claims.text: The proposed approach will calculate lattice and electronic thermal conductivity separately for HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed approach will improve predictive accuracy by at least approximately 20% relative to earlier methods.
Previous simulations of HfNbTaTiZr employed a defect-free bulk crystalline state.
Anharmonic DFT can explicitly calculate temperature-dependent phonon lifetimes while capturing atomic-scale disorder in HfNbTaTiZr.
Electron–phonon coupling calculations can independently determine electronic scattering rates in HfNbTaTiZr.
Combining the two calculations will yield distinct lattice and electronic thermal conductivities without conflating them.
The approach is applicable to nearly pristine HfNbTaTiZr from approximately 200 K to 1200 K.
The influence of oxygen on high-temperature conductivity can be represented as an additive correction to the pristine-alloy prediction.
Atomic-scale disorder and anisotropy in force constants affect phonon scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Atomic-scale disorder and force-constant anisotropy affect electron–phonon interactions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Directly calculating phonon anharmonicity and electron scattering without a Debye-temperature fitting parameter will outperform earlier analytical approaches.
Separating lattice and electronic pathways will permit more accurate quantification and independent experimental validation of both pathways.
Lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable below 200 K.
The total thermal conductivity of oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr is approximately 10–17 W/(K m) at 300–1200 K.
The predicted lattice thermal conductivity will deviate by less than 20% from an experimentally decoupled lattice contribution below 200 K.
After oxygen-related modification, predicted total conductivity over 300–1200 K will remain within 10–17 W/(K m).
Earlier analytical and DFT-based models have errors exceeding 20% relative to experiment.
Above 1200 K, severe defect activation or phase instability may invalidate the predictions.
Time-domain thermoreflectance or differential 3ω measurements can independently resolve lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K.

contradictions.description: The stated predictive applicability begins at approximately 200 K, but the principal quantified lattice-conductivity prediction and falsification threshold are defined below 200 K, outside that stated range.

The predicted outcome calls for matching high-temperature conductivity trends, whereas the falsification rule only requires values to fall somewhere within the broad 10–17 W/(K m) range; satisfying the latter does not establish agreement with the temperature-dependent trend.
